extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in law, free speech, and online social-media moderation (legal scholars, journalists, civics-interested public)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how social-media platforms (here, Twitter) apply moderation rules to satirical content that targets individuals or protected classes, and the legal/policy constraints affecting those decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitter hateful conduct prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's rules ban promoting violence against, threatening, or harassing other people on the basis of protected characteristics, including gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied broadly to conduct that targets people for protected characteristics; used by Twitter to justify enforcement actions such as suspensions. (Page quote: rules "against hateful conduct," which ban "promot[ing] violence against, threaten[ing], or harass[ing] other people on the basis of," among other things, gender identity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted misgendering or deadnaming is prohibited
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter's policy explicitly states that targeted misgendering or deadnaming of transgender individuals is included in the hateful-conduct prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specific inclusion means that even satirical or ideological statements that intentionally call a transgender person by an incorrect gender or former name can be treated as policy violations. (Page quote: "This includes targeted misgendering or deadnaming of transgender individuals.")

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical content can be treated as harassment when it targets protected characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire or ideological criticism that refers to a transgender person using the wrong gender (or otherwise targets their gender identity) may violate platform harassment/hate policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page uses the Babylon Bee tweet (calling Rachel Levine 'Man of the Year') as an example where Twitter appears to classify the satire as hateful conduct; this indicates platforms may not exempt satire from enforcement when it targets protected traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement mechanics: temporary suspension conditional on deletion
rubrics_metrics.description: The reported enforcement in this case was a 12-hour ban that would be lifted only if the offending tweet were deleted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical compliance requirement for account holders: deletion of specific content may be required to regain access; refusal to delete can result in continued suspension or loss of account (illustrated by the Babylon Bee CEO's refusal to delete the tweet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private-platform free-speech limitation (First Amendment inapplicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Twitter is a private company, it is not constrained by the First Amendment in choosing what speech to permit or remove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts have sometimes described social-media platforms as the "modern public square," current federal law does not stop private platforms from setting and enforcing their own content rules; state statutes attempting to constrain platforms exist but are being challenged and sometimes preliminarily blocked by courts. The page suggests monitoring platform constraints even if legal remedies are uncertain.
